Economics - North America
Hawkward Pause

- We now expect the Fed to remain on hold indefinitely (versus our prior forecast of two cuts in September and December). Incoming Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is likely still motivated to cut rates. However, we expect easing political pressure, elevated inflation, and strong cyclical growth to support a prolonged pause.

- Data have remained relatively hawkish lately. Growth has remained robust due to strong investment and steady consumption. Labor markets appear to be stabilizing, while both survey and hard data point to building price pressures.
We now expect the Fed to keep policy rates unchanged indefinitely, versus our previous forecast for two cuts in September and December (Fig. 1 & 2).

Political pressure for near-term rate cuts has diminished recently. Tariff inflation has begun to fade, but new price pressures have emerged from the Iran war and global memory chip shortages. Additionally, although we think Warsh would be inclined to ease policy, support among Fed officials for an easing bias has begun to wane.

Political pressures for imminent rate cuts appear to have eased. According to his interview with Fortune Magazine which was published on Monday this week, President Trump has appeared resigned to giving up on rate cuts for some time, saying "You can't really look at the figures until the war is over." Moreover, reportedly, Trump is unlikely to put pressures on the new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh in a specific direction as he mentioned "I'm going to let him do what he wants to do."

Recent Fedspeak shows even dovish officials are no longer advocating for rate cuts or an easing bias. Governor Waller was hawkish in his remarks, where he cited inflation risks, mentioned that labor markets were stabilizing with few risks of deterioration and called for

removing the easing bias. He expressed concerns about the breadth of increases in consumer prices and sharp increases in PPI. Moreover, he mentioned that a series of transitory shocks could lead to persistent inflation, and consequently he viewed a rate cut was no more likely than a hike. Philly Fed President Paulson also leaned hawkish and endorsed market expectations for the policy rate, saying “the way the market has moved in reaction to economic news over the last few months largely aligns with my own thinking” and it was “healthy” that traders were pricing in a long pause or even rate hikes. She also appeared comfortable removing forward guidance at the June FOMC statement.

The April FOMC meeting minutes were relatively hawkish, consistent with Powell's messaging at the post-meeting press conference. As we had expected, the number of officials supporting a change to the easing bias increased to "many" from "some" in March and "several" in January (Fig. 3).

Data remain hawkish, pointing to robust growth and building price pressures

Manufacturing and business capex continue to accelerate. The preliminary S&P Manufacturing PMI rose to a multi-year high. Elevated uncertainty has had little visible impact on manufacturing or capex, which continues to accelerate and broaden beyond tech/AI. Capital goods shipments and imports have also strengthened. We expect durable goods orders rose \(4.8\%\) m-o-m in April, driven by broad-based gains. Excluding the volatile transportation component, orders likely rose \(0.9\%\), while core capital goods shipments advanced \(1.0\%\). Incorporating this week's data and our forecasts for next week, our Q2 GDP tracking stands at \(2.6\%\) q-o-q ar, one-tenth lower than last week, while real final sales to private domestic purchasers remain unchanged at \(2.9\%\) q-o-q ar.

Housing demand has also remained resilient despite elevated mortgage rates. Pending home sales surprised to the upside, rising \(1.4\%\) m-o-m (Nomura and Consensus: \(1.0\%\)) after an upwardly revised \(1.7\%\) gain in March. Starts and permits held steady, though due to volatile multifamily segment. The NAHB survey also showed firmer six-month sales expectations and buyer traffic.

Labor market data continue to point to accelerating job gains. ADP's weekly data suggest private payrolls rose an average of 42.5k per week in the four weeks ending 2 May from 33.0k previously, the highest in the series history (Fig. 4). The level of claims has been mostly sideways recently, which we view as incrementally positive news, given the seasonal tendency in recent years of initial claims rising into the summer (Fig. 5).

At the same time, survey data point to intensifying price pressures. The S&P Manufacturing PMI input price index surged to 79.5 in May from 68.4, the largest monthly increase in the series history (Fig. 6). The NY Fed services price index also continued to rise, signaling persistent supercore PCE inflation (Fig. 7). Consumer inflation expectations also remained elevated, as the final reading of the UMich long-term inflation expectations jumped sharply to \(3.9\%\) in May from its preliminary print of \(3.4\%\).

We expect core PCE inflation to rise \(0.300\%\) m-o-m in April, up from \(0.293\%\) in March. This translates to a y-o-y change of \(3.3\%\) in April, up from \(3.2\%\) in March. Core goods inflation likely rose for the fifth consecutive month, led by computer software and accessories. Looking ahead, we expect further price pressures on electronics due to the global shortage of semiconductors. Supercore PCE likely slowed in April due to softer financial and healthcare services, but strong equity markets point to a rebound in financial services prices in May. Airline fares also likely accelerated in April and are likely to continue pushing core PCE higher in coming months.

Data Preview
The week ahead
We expect core PCE accelerated in April, pointing to building price pressures.

Consumer confidence (Tuesday): We expect the Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index edged down to 92.3 in May from 92.8 in April. High frequency data from Morning Consult and the SF Daily News Sentiment Index suggest sentiment remained low. Stock prices rose, but the increase in energy prices likely kept consumers pessimistic.

Jobless claims (Thursday): Initial claims ticked down this week, while continuing claims picked up. The level of claims has been mostly sideways recently, which we view as incrementally positive news given the seasonal tendency in recent years of initial claims rising into the summer.

Personal income and spending (Thursday): We expect personal income growth slowed to \(0.4\%\) in April from \(0.6\%\) in March. Compensation of employees picked up due to a rebound in private payroll income. However, this was more than offset by a moderation in proprietors' income. This component is typically strong in March and tends to revert lower in subsequent months. Personal income receipts on assets also likely ticked down.

We expect personal spending growth edged down to \(0.6\%\) m-o-m in April from \(0.9\%\) in March. Retail sales slowed in the month suggesting a moderation in goods spending. Energy-related spending remained elevated. Based on our PCE inflation estimates, we expect real personal spending grew \(0.2\%\) m-o-m.

PCE deflator (Thursday): Incorporating relevant details from CPI, PPI, and import prices, we expect core PCE inflation accelerated to \(0.300\%\) m-o-m in April from \(0.293\%\) in March. This translates to a y-o-y change of \(3.3\%\) in April, up from \(3.2\%\) in March.

We expect PCE core goods inflation remained strong in April, the fifth consecutive monthly increase, primarily driven by higher computer software & accessories prices. Looking ahead, we expect further price pressures on electronics due to the global shortage of semiconductors.

Supercore PCE inflation likely decelerated in April, largely due to softness in financial service and healthcare service prices. However, recent strong equity market performance points to a rebound in PCE's financial service prices in May. Airline fares accelerated and are likely to continue rising, pushing up core PCE inflation in coming months.

Overall, another \(0.3\%\) reading of core PCE inflation, along with forward-looking price pressures, suggests that the hawkish macroeconomic environment will persist well into the second half of this year. This supports our Fed call for an indefinite hold.

GDP Q1 second estimate (Thursday): We expect the second estimate of Q1 GDP to be unchanged from its initial release of \(2.0\%\) q-o-q ar, with changes to the composition of growth. We expect real final sales to private domestic purchasers will be revised up to \(1.7\%\) q-o-q ar from its initial release of \(1.6\%\). Q1 PCE is likely to be revised up as retail sales were revised higher for March. Construction spending came in stronger in February and March, which is likely to drive up fixed investment. On the other hand, trade data suggest net exports were lower than the BEA's initial assumption.

Durable goods orders (Thursday): We expect durable goods orders rose \(4.8\%\) m-o-m in April following a \(0.8\%\) increase in March. Nondefense aircraft orders likely picked up as Boeing net orders increased sharply. Defense orders and motor vehicles and parts orders also likely grew in the month.

Excluding volatile transportation equipment, durable goods orders likely remained strong at \(0.9\%\) m-o-m. Industrial production for durable goods excluding motor vehicles rose, and new order indices of manufacturing surveys increased further. We expect core capital goods shipments, an input into GDP's equipment investment, grew \(1.0\%\) m-o-m in April.

New home sales (Thursday): We expect the pace of new home sales slowed to 665k in April from 682k in March. Higher mortgage rates and Iran war-related uncertainty kept buyers on the sidelines. The NAHB survey indicated that new home sales declined in the month.
Advance goods trade balance (Friday): We expect the advance goods trade deficit

US Economic Outlook
We expect the Fed to stay on hold indefinitely due to diminished political pressure, elevated inflation, and hawkish Fedspeak.

Economic activity: Growth momentum has accelerated, supported by easing tariff uncertainty, fiscal stimulus from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and the lagged impact of Fed rate cuts amid easy financial conditions. Business investment appears to be broadening beyond the AI sector. Higher tax refunds and strong payroll income growth has supported consumer spending thus far, despite headwinds from the Iran war. A broad range of indicators point to resilience and tentative signs of reacceleration in the labor market. We expect the unemployment rate will begin to decline, reaching \(4.1\%\) by year-end. We think that the US economy remains relatively insulated from the crude oil price shock due to the Iran war given the small share of energy-goods consumption in household spending, as well as domestic energy production.

Inflation: Core inflation remains well above the Fed's \(2\%\) target, and we believe risks are skewed to the upside. We forecast Q4 2026 core PCE inflation of \(3.3\%\) y-o-y. We expect tariff price pressures will diminish in the coming quarters. However, supply shortages caused by AI (memory chips, electricity, etc.) along with higher metal prices could exert new inflationary pressures on goods prices. Wage growth seems to have leveled off around \(4\%\), which is likely to lead to stickiness in supercore service inflation. We expect rent disinflation to continue, but at a very gradual pace.

Policy: We expect the Fed to remain on hold indefinitely. Fed Chair Warsh likely remains motivated to ease policy, but recent elevated inflation readings and hawkish Fedspeak make us skeptical that he will be able to convince a majority of the Fed to go along with rate cuts. Moreover, support among Fed officials for an easing bias has begun to wane. While hikes are not likely in the near term, the Fed's hesitance to respond to tentative signs of an inflation problem increases the risk that they may end up "behind the curve," needing to hike quickly to re-establish credibility. On tariffs, wider Section 122 exemptions, lower tariff rates, and a greater focus on affordability suggest limited further escalation in US trade policy.

Risks: Further escalation of geopolitical risks could lead to a tightening of financial conditions and worsening of the fiscal outlook. Increased political pressures on individual FOMC participants could undermine the Fed's credibility, soliciting sharp market reactions. A bust of the AI boom could lead to material corrections in asset valuations. A continued shortage of memory chips and supply chain disruption due to a protracted Iran war could lead to a second round of goods price increases.
